claim: ANE syndrome is a ribosomopathy caused by a mutation in an RNA recognition motif of RBM28.
source: ANE syndrome is a ribosomopathy caused by a mutation in an RNA recognition motif of RBM28, a nucleolar protein conserved to yeast (Nop4).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to prior work (Nousbeck et al., 2008) establishing ANE syndrome as a ribosomopathy.

claim: RBM28 is a nucleolar protein conserved to yeast (Nop4).
source: ANE syndrome is a ribosomopathy caused by a mutation in an RNA recognition motif of RBM28, a nucleolar protein conserved to yeast (Nop4).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and reflects established knowledge about the conservation of RBM28.

claim: Patients with ANE syndrome have fewer mature ribosomes.
source: While patients with ANE syndrome have fewer mature ribosomes, it is unclear how this mutation disrupts ribosome assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to Nousbeck et al., 2008 elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Nop4 is a hub protein in the nucleolar large subunit (LSU) processome interactome.
source: Recently, we found that Nop4 is a hub protein in the nucleolar large subunit (LSU) processome interactome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to the authors' recent work (McCann et al., 2015).

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation in yeast Nop4 (L306P) confers growth defects.
source: Here we use yeast as a model system and show that the mutation confers growth and pre-rRNA processing defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation in yeast Nop4 (L306P) confers pre-rRNA processing defects.
source: Here we use yeast as a model system and show that the mutation confers growth and pre-rRNA processing defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation disrupts Nop4's hub function by abrogating several of Nop4's protein-protein interactions.
source: Here we demonstrate that the ANE syndrome mutation disrupts Nop4's hub function by abrogating several of Nop4's protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Y2H and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation in RRM3 of human RBM28 disrupts domain folding as demonstrated by circular dichroism.
source: Circular dichroism and NMR demonstrate that the ANE syndrome mutation in RRM3 of human RBM28 disrupts domain folding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CD data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation in RRM3 of human RBM28 disrupts domain folding as demonstrated by NMR.
source: Circular dichroism and NMR demonstrate that the ANE syndrome mutation in RRM3 of human RBM28 disrupts domain folding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation generates defective protein folding which abrogates protein-protein interactions.
source: We conclude that the ANE syndrome mutation generates defective protein folding which abrogates protein-protein interactions and causes faulty pre-LSU rRNA processing, thus revealing one aspect of the molecular basis of this human disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, integrating findings from structural and functional studies.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation causes faulty pre-LSU rRNA processing.
source: We conclude that the ANE syndrome mutation generates defective protein folding which abrogates protein-protein interactions and causes faulty pre-LSU rRNA processing, thus revealing one aspect of the molecular basis of this human disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pre-rRNA processing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis requires the coordinated action of all three RNA polymerases.
source: The fundamental cellular process of ribosome assembly requires the coordinated action of all three RNA polymerases, over 200 biogenesis factors, and a number of small nucleolar RNAs (Thomson et al., 2013; Woolford and Baserga, 2013; Fernández-Pevida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis requires over 200 biogenesis factors.
source: The fundamental cellular process of ribosome assembly requires the coordinated action of all three RNA polymerases, over 200 biogenesis factors, and a number of small nucleolar RNAs (Thomson et al., 2013; Woolford and Baserga, 2013; Fernández-Pevida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis requires a number of small nucleolar RNAs.
source: The fundamental cellular process of ribosome assembly requires the coordinated action of all three RNA polymerases, over 200 biogenesis factors, and a number of small nucleolar RNAs (Thomson et al., 2013; Woolford and Baserga, 2013; Fernández-Pevida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In yeast, ribosome biogenesis initiates in the nucleolus with the transcription of the 35S polycistronic pre-ribosomal RNA precursor by RNA polymerase I.
source: In yeast, ribosome biogenesis initiates in the nucleolus with the transcription of the 35S polycistronic pre-ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor by RNA polymerase I.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and reflects established knowledge about yeast ribosome biogenesis.

claim: The 35S pre-rRNA undergoes cleavage and modification events to give rise to the mature 18S, 5.8S and 25S rRNAs.
source: The 35S pre-rRNA undergoes a number of cleavage and modification events to give rise to the mature 18S, 5.8S and 25S rRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and reflects established knowledge about pre-rRNA processing.

claim: Mutations that partially disrupt ribosome assembly or function can lead to disease in humans.
source: Mutations that partially disrupt ribosome assembly or function are often deleterious and can lead to disease in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and reflects established knowledge about ribosomopathies.

claim: Diseases of ribosome biogenesis are called ribosomopathies.
source: Collectively, these diseases of ribosome biogenesis are called ribosomopathies.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and reflects established terminology.

claim: Ribosomopathies are caused by mutations in proteins that function in all stages of ribosome assembly.
source: Ribosomopathies are caused by mutations in proteins that function in all stages of ribosome assembly (McCann and Baserga, 2013; Armistead and Triggs-Raine, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to review literature.

claim: A homozygous missense mutation in RBM28 causes ANE syndrome.
source: A homozygous missense mutation in the nucleolar protein RBM28 causes the ribosomopathy, alopecia, neurological defects and endocrinopathy (ANE) syndrome (Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Nousbeck et al., 2008.

claim: Five affected children of a consanguineous kindred displayed degrees of baldness, mental retardation, motor deterioration, and reduced pituitary gland function in their second decade of life.
source: Five affected children of a consanguineous kindred displayed degrees of baldness, mental retardation, motor deterioration, and reduced pituitary gland function in their second decade of life (Nousbeck et al., 2008; Warshauer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to clinical reports.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation segregated in the family in an autosomal recessive manner.
source: The mutation segregated in the family in an autosomal recessive manner and was mapped to a single leucine to proline amino acid substitution at position 351 (L351P) of RBM28.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Nousbeck et al., 2008.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation was mapped to a single leucine to proline amino acid substitution at position 351 (L351P) of RBM28.
source: The mutation segregated in the family in an autosomal recessive manner and was mapped to a single leucine to proline amino acid substitution at position 351 (L351P) of RBM28.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Nousbeck et al., 2008.

claim: The L351P residue resides in the first α-helix of RBM28's third RNA recognition motif (RRM3).
source: This residue resides in the first α-helix of its third RNA recognition motif (RRM3; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by structural information shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ANE syndrome was classified as a ribosomopathy because RBM28 is localized to the nucleolus.
source: ANE syndrome was classified as a ribosomopathy because RBM28 is localized to the nucleolus and because patient fibroblasts showed reduced numbers of ribosomes (Damianov et al., 2006; Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ANE syndrome was classified as a ribosomopathy because patient fibroblasts showed reduced numbers of ribosomes.
source: ANE syndrome was classified as a ribosomopathy because RBM28 is localized to the nucleolus and because patient fibroblasts showed reduced numbers of ribosomes (Damianov et al., 2006; Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The L351P mutation is predicted to disrupt the first α-helix of RRM3.
source: While the L351P mutation is predicted to disrupt the first α-helix of RRM3 and thereby impair RBM28 function, it is not known how this single amino acid substitution disrupts the normal function of RBM28 in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on structural predictions.

claim: Nop4 is the yeast ortholog of RBM28.
source: Nop4, the yeast ortholog of RBM28, is required for assembly of the large ribosomal subunit (LSU; Bergès et al., 1994; Sun and Woolford, 1994; Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nop4 is required for assembly of the large ribosomal subunit (LSU).
source: Nop4, the yeast ortholog of RBM28, is required for assembly of the large ribosomal subunit (LSU; Bergès et al., 1994; Sun and Woolford, 1994; Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The LSU processome interactome revealed that Nop4 functions as a hub protein.
source: Recently, the LSU processome interactome revealed that Nop4 functions as a hub protein, interacting with many more proteins than average within the LSU processome (McCann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Nop4 interacts with many more proteins than average within the LSU processome.
source: Recently, the LSU processome interactome revealed that Nop4 functions as a hub protein, interacting with many more proteins than average within the LSU processome (McCann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Nop4 L306P has a doubling time of 7.8 hours compared to 4.8 hours for Nop4 WT in liquid medium at 23°C.
source: Similar to growth on solid medium, Nop4 L306P exhibited a moderate growth defect in liquid culture, doubling every 7.8 hr, compared to WT, which doubled every 4.8 hr; however, the defect was not as severe as that observed with the EV control, which doubled every 20.5 hr (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The mature 25S rRNA and the 27S and 7S pre-rRNA precursors are severely reduced in yeast depleted of Nop4.
source: Previously, it has been shown that the mature 25S rRNA and the 27S and 7S pre-rRNA precursors are severely reduced in yeast depleted of Nop4 (Figure 2A; Bergès et al., 1994; Sun and Woolford, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nop4 L306P confers a statistically significant reduction in the 25S/18S rRNA ratio.
source: Nop4 L306P conferred a moderate growth defect and a moderate, but statistically significant, reduction in the 25S/18S rRNA ratio (Figure 2C), consistent with reduced 25S levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Depletion of Nop4 results in a severe reduction of 27S and 7S levels.
source: Depletion of Nop4 (EV) resulted in a severe reduction of 27S and 7S levels, with a concomitant decrease in the 27S/35S, 7S/35S, 27S/Scr1 and 7S/Scr1 ratios, indicative of an ITS1 processing defect, as has been previously observed (Figure 2B,C; Bergès et al., 1994; Sun and Woolford, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B,C, with support from prior citations.

claim: The Nop4 L306P mutant displays a statistically significant ITS1 processing defect as indicated by reduced 27S/35S, 7S/35S and 7S/Scr1 ratios.
source: The Nop4 L306P mutant showed an intermediate growth defect and also displayed an intermediate, but statistically significant, ITS1 processing defect as indicated by reduced 27S/35S, 7S/35S and 7S/Scr1 ratios (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B,C with statistical analysis.

claim: The ANE mutation in Nop4 (L306P) abrogates interaction with Mak5 by Y2H.
source: While all 5 bait proteins interacted with Nop4 WT, as indicated by growth on SD-Leu-Trp-His + 6 mM 3-AT, Mak5, Nop4, and Nsa2 did not interact with Nop4 L306P, as no growth was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H assay in Figure 3C.

claim: The ANE mutation in Nop4 (L306P) abrogates interaction with Nop4 itself by Y2H.
source: While all 5 bait proteins interacted with Nop4 WT, as indicated by growth on SD-Leu-Trp-His + 6 mM 3-AT, Mak5, Nop4, and Nsa2 did not interact with Nop4 L306P, as no growth was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H assay in Figure 3C.

claim: The ANE mutation in Nop4 (L306P) abrogates interaction with Nsa2 by Y2H.
source: While all 5 bait proteins interacted with Nop4 WT, as indicated by growth on SD-Leu-Trp-His + 6 mM 3-AT, Mak5, Nop4, and Nsa2 did not interact with Nop4 L306P, as no growth was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H assay in Figure 3C.

claim: Noc2 interacts with Nop4 L306P by Y2H, but growth is reduced compared to WT.
source: Noc2 did interact with Nop4 L306P, but growth was reduced compared to WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H assay in Figure 3C.

claim: Dbp10 interaction with Nop4 is unaffected by the L306P mutation.
source: In contrast, Dbp10 interaction with Nop4 was unaffected by the L306P mutation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H assay in Figure 3C.

claim: 3xHA-Nop4 L306P co-purifies significantly less efficiently than 3xHA-Nop4 WT with all interacting partners assayed except Dbp10.
source: Interestingly, 3xHA-Nop4 L306P co-purified significantly less efficiently than 3xHA-Nop4 WT with all interacting partners assayed, except Dbp10, as was observed by Y2H.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation disrupts or reduces a subset of Nop4 protein-protein interactions.
source: Thus, the ANE syndrome mutation disrupts or reduces a subset of Nop4 protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Y2H and co-IP data in Figure 3.

claim: RRM domains typically bind RNA.
source: Although RRM domains typically bind RNA, there are several published examples of RRMs that bind proteins rather than RNA (Fribourg et al., 2003; Lau et al., 2003; Selenko et al., 2003; Bono et al., 2004; Kadlec et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and reflects established knowledge about RRM domains.

claim: There are several published examples of RRMs that bind proteins rather than RNA.
source: Although RRM domains typically bind RNA, there are several published examples of RRMs that bind proteins rather than RNA (Fribourg et al., 2003; Lau et al., 2003; Selenko et al., 2003; Bono et al., 2004; Kadlec et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nop4 RRM 3-4 mediates protein-protein interactions.
source: We found that Nop4 RRM 3–4 mediated the protein-protein interactions observed in the LSU processome interactome using a directed Y2H assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H data in Figure 4C.

claim: Nop4 RRM 1-2 did not interact with any of the Nop4 interacting proteins by Y2H.
source: To our surprise, Nop4 RRM 1–2 did not interact with any of the Nop4 interacting proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H data in Figure 4C.

claim: Nop4 RRM 3-4 interacted with the majority of the defined interacting set of proteins, similar to the full-length Nop4 WT.
source: In contrast, Nop4 RRM 3–4 interacted with the majority of the defined interacting set of proteins, similar to the full-length Nop4 WT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the Y2H data in Figure 4C.

claim: Nop4 RRMs 3 and 4 are necessary and sufficient for protein-protein interactions.
source: Thus, Nop4 RRMs 3 and 4 are necessary and sufficient for these protein-protein interactions and are thereby likely to mediate Nop4's function as a hub protein in the LSU processome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Y2H data in Figure 4C.

claim: Nop4 RRMs 3 and 4 are likely to mediate Nop4's function as a hub protein in the LSU processome.
source: Thus, Nop4 RRMs 3 and 4 are necessary and sufficient for these protein-protein interactions and are thereby likely to mediate Nop4's function as a hub protein in the LSU processome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the Y2H data in Figure 4C.

claim: Nop4 RRM 3-4 is sufficient to complement the growth defect observed upon Nop4 depletion.
source: Nop4 RRM 3–4 is also sufficient to complement the growth defect observed upon Nop4 depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the growth assays in Figure 5B,C,D.

claim: Nop4 RRM 3-4 complemented the growth defect at 23°C and 17°C and partially complemented at 30°C.
source: However, Nop4 RRM 3–4 complemented the growth defect at 23°C and 17°C and partially complemented at 30°C (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the growth assay in Figure 5B.

claim: Nop4 RRM 1-2 did not complement the growth defect at any temperature tested.
source: Like EV, Nop4 RRM 1–2 did not complement the growth defect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the growth assay in Figure 5B.

claim: The failure of Nop4 RRM 1-2 to complement the growth defect is not due to aberrant localization of the protein fragment.
source: The failure of Nop4 RRM 1–2 to complement the growth defect is not due to aberrant localization of the protein fragment. Nop4 RRM 1–2 also fails to complement when expressed from the yeast two-hybrid vector, pACT2, which ensures targeting of the fragment to the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting that this domain is not essential for Nop4 function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the immunofluorescence and growth data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The essential function of Nop4 is mediated through RRMs 3 and 4.
source: In contrast, the ability of Nop4 RRM 3–4 to complement the growth defect in both solid and liquid medium suggests that the essential function of Nop4 is mediated through RRMs 3 and 4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the complementation data in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of Nop4 RRM 3-4 is sufficient to partially restore pre-rRNA processing.
source: Expression of Nop4 RRM 3–4 is sufficient to partially restore pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the pre-rRNA processing data in Figure 6.

claim: Nop4 RRM 3-4 significantly rescued the 25S/18S ratio compared to EV at 23°C, but not at 30°C.
source: In contrast, Nop4 RRM 3–4 was sufficient to significantly rescue the 25S/18S ratio compared to EV at 23°C, but not at 30°C (Figure 6B), consistent with a restoration of 25S levels at 23°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: Expression of Nop4 RRM 3-4, but not Nop4 RRM 1-2, significantly restored the levels of the 27S and 7S intermediates at 23°C but failed to rescue at 30°C.
source: Strikingly, expression of Nop4 RRM 3–4, but not Nop4 RRM 1–2, significantly restored the levels of the 27S and 7S intermediates at 23°C but failed to rescue at 30°C (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: The essential function of Nop4 in ribosome assembly is mediated through the protein binding RRMs, RRM3 and RRM4.
source: Thus, pre-rRNA processing parallels the observed growth complementation and suggests that the essential function of Nop4 in ribosome assembly is mediated through the protein binding RRMs, RRM3 and RRM4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the complementation and pre-rRNA processing data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The L351P mutation disrupts the backbone structure of the RBM28 RRM3 domain.
source: We found that the L351P mutation disrupts the backbone structure of the RBM28 RRM3 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown by CD data in Figure 7A.

claim: The CD spectra of WT and L351P RBM28 RRM3 showed notable differences in ellipticities [θ] at 208, 215 and 222 nm.
source: The CD spectra of WT and L351P RBM28 RRM3 showed notable differences in ellipticities [θ] at 208, 215 and 222 nm (Figure 7A), indicating that the amino acid substitution reduced α-helical and β-sheet content.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The amino acid substitution L351P reduced α-helical and β-sheet content in RBM28 RRM3.
source: The CD spectra of WT and L351P RBM28 RRM3 showed notable differences in ellipticities [θ] at 208, 215 and 222 nm (Figure 7A), indicating that the amino acid substitution reduced α-helical and β-sheet content.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an interpretation of the CD data in Figure 7A.

claim: The CD spectrum of the L351P mutant protein with a minimum only at ~200 nm indicated the presence of random coil.
source: The CD spectrum of the L351P mutant protein with a minimum only at ~200 nm indicated the presence of random coil.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an interpretation of the CD data in Figure 7A.

claim: 15N-HSQC of WT RBM28 RRM3 showed well dispersed resonances, indicating the presence of both α-helices and β-strands.
source: 15N-HSQC of WT RBM28 RRM3 showed well dispersed resonances (Figure 7B), indicating the presence of both α-helices and β-strands, as expected for an RRM domain(Nagai et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B, with support from citation to Nagai et al., 1990.

claim: The majority of resonances in the spectrum of L351P ANE syndrome mutant RRM3 were clustered around 8.0~8.5 ppm in the proton dimension, demonstrating that the mutant protein backbone is disordered.
source: In contrast, the majority of resonances in the spectrum of L351P ANE syndrome mutant RRM3 were clustered around 8.0~8.5 ppm in the proton dimension, demonstrating that the mutant protein backbone is disordered.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: L351 is buried within the core of the RBM28 RRM3 domain.
source: A homology model of the human RBM28 RRM3, based on an NMR structure of mouse RBM28 RRM3, indicates that L351 is buried within the core of the domain (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the homology model in Figure 7C.

claim: Mutation of L351 to proline would be expected to disrupt helix α1 and the overall tertiary structure of RBM28 RRM3.
source: Mutation to proline would be expected to disrupt helix α1 and the overall tertiary structure of this RRM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is an inference based on the structural model and known properties of proline.

claim: The molecular pathogenesis of ANE syndrome results from disrupted RRM3 protein structure that reduces its function as a hub protein in the LSU processome.
source: We determined that the molecular pathogenesis of ANE syndrome (L351P in the nucleolar protein, RBM28) results from disrupted RRM3 protein structure that reduces its function as a hub protein in the LSU processome and causes defects in pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is the main conclusion integrating all findings.

claim: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes growth defects.
source: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes growth and pre-rRNA processing defects, as well as reduced association with interacting protein partners.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes pre-rRNA processing defects.
source: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes growth and pre-rRNA processing defects, as well as reduced association with interacting protein partners.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes reduced association with interacting protein partners.
source: Introducing the ANE syndrome mutation into RRM3 of the yeast ortholog, Nop4 (L306P), causes growth and pre-rRNA processing defects, as well as reduced association with interacting protein partners.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for Nop4 protein-protein interactions.
source: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for Nop4 protein-protein interactions and for yeast growth and pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for yeast growth.
source: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for Nop4 protein-protein interactions and for yeast growth and pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for pre-rRNA processing.
source: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 alone are necessary and sufficient for Nop4 protein-protein interactions and for yeast growth and pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Biophysical methods indicate that RRM3 containing the ANE syndrome mutation is unfolded.
source: Biophysical methods indicate that RRM3 containing the ANE syndrome mutation is unfolded.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by CD and NMR data in Figure 7.

claim: ANE syndrome is a ribosomopathy with a molecular defect in nucleolar steps of ribosome biogenesis.
source: Taken together, these results provide evidence that ANE syndrome is a ribosomopathy with a molecular defect in nucleolar steps of ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The finding that an essential function of Nop4 is to mediate protein binding was unexpected.
source: The finding that an essential function of Nop4 is to mediate protein binding was unexpected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and reflects the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Nop4 has been cross-linked to pre-rRNA.
source: Nop4 has been cross-linked to pre-rRNA (Bergès et al., 1994; Sun and Woolford, 1994; Granneman et al., 2011), leading to the expectation that its 4 RRMs would be essential for RNA binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The C-terminal half of Nop4 (RRMs 3 and 4) mediates protein-protein interactions and hub protein function in the LSU processome.
source: We show by Y2H analysis that the C-terminal half of Nop4 (RRMs 3 and 4) mediates protein-protein interactions and hub protein function in the LSU processome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by Y2H data in Figure 4.

claim: The C-terminal half of Nop4 (RRMs 3 and 4) is necessary and sufficient to complement the growth and pre-rRNA processing defects observed upon depletion of endogenous Nop4.
source: Strikingly, this half of Nop4 is necessary and sufficient to complement the growth and pre-rRNA processing defects observed upon depletion of endogenous Nop4.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: ANE syndrome is likely a disease of altered protein interaction rather than of RNA binding.
source: As the ANE syndrome mutation occurs in RRM3 and disrupts Nop4 protein-protein interactions, ANE syndrome is therefore likely a disease of altered protein interaction rather than of RNA binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is an inference based on the findings that the mutation disrupts protein interactions.

claim: Nop4 binds RNA in vitro.
source: Nop4 binds RNA in vitro (Sun and Woolford, 1997), co-immunoprecipitates the 27S and 7S pre-rRNAs and crosslinks to the 25S within the pre-rRNA in vivo (Granneman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Sun and Woolford, 1997.

claim: Nop4 co-immunoprecipitates the 27S and 7S pre-rRNAs.
source: Nop4 binds RNA in vitro (Sun and Woolford, 1997), co-immunoprecipitates the 27S and 7S pre-rRNAs and crosslinks to the 25S within the pre-rRNA in vivo (Granneman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Granneman et al., 2011.

claim: Nop4 crosslinks to the 25S within the pre-rRNA in vivo.
source: Nop4 binds RNA in vitro (Sun and Woolford, 1997), co-immunoprecipitates the 27S and 7S pre-rRNAs and crosslinks to the 25S within the pre-rRNA in vivo (Granneman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Granneman et al., 2011.

claim: All 4 RRMs of Nop4 are important for Nop4 function as mutations in any of the RRMs disrupt growth and LSU assembly at 37°C.
source: Additionally, all 4 RRMs are important for Nop4 function as mutations in any of the RRMs disrupt growth and LSU assembly at 37°C (Sun and Woolford, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Sun and Woolford, 1997.

claim: RRMs 1 and 2 of Nop4 may bind the pre-rRNA.
source: Although RRMs 1 and 2 are not required for Nop4's hub protein function or sufficient for growth, they may bind the pre-rRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is speculation based on the findings.

claim: The possibility that RRMs 3 and 4 may also bind RNA is not precluded.
source: Furthermore, while RRMs 3 and 4 mediate protein binding, the possibility that they may also bind RNA is not precluded.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is speculation.

claim: Several examples of RRMs mediating interactions with other proteins have been identified including in the U2AF35-U2AF65, the U2AF65-SF1, the Snu17-Bud13, and the Y14-Mago complexes.
source: Several examples of RRMs mediating interactions with other proteins have been identified including in the U2AF35-U2AF65, the U2AF65-SF1, the Snu17-Bud13, and the Y14-Mago complexes (Kielkopf et al., 2001; Fribourg et al., 2003; Lau et al., 2003; Selenko et al., 2003; Tripsianes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An RRM is comprised of a 4-stranded β-sheet, which forms the primary RNA binding interface, and 2 α-helices.
source: An RRM is comprised of a 4-stranded β-sheet, which forms the primary RNA binding interface, and 2 α-helices (Maris et al., 2005; Cléry et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior work describing RRM structure.

claim: The α-helices of the RRM often mediate interaction between protein pairs, leaving the β-sheet accessible for RNA binding.
source: The α-helices of the RRM often mediate interaction between protein pairs, leaving the β-sheet accessible for RNA binding (Kielkopf et al., 2001; Selenko et al., 2003; Tripsianes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the case of the Y14-Mago complex, the interaction is through the β-sheet, which precludes RNA binding.
source: Alternatively, in the case of the Y14-Mago complex, the interaction is through the β-sheet, which precludes RNA binding (Fribourg et al., 2003; Lau et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RRMs can serve as oligomerization domains.
source: RRMs also can serve as oligomerization domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and reflects established knowledge about RRM function.

claim: In the case of Human antigen R (HuR), the third RRM promotes dimerization through its α-helices.
source: In the case of Human antigen R (HuR), the third RRM promotes dimerization through its α-helices (Scheiba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Scheiba et al., 2014.

claim: RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 may mediate protein binding and hub function through more than one of its structural motifs.
source: These examples highlight the possibility that RRMs 3 and 4 of Nop4 may mediate protein binding and hub function through more than one of its structural motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is speculation based on the examples provided.

claim: The ANE mutation lies in an α-helix and the mutation disrupts not only the α-helix, but unfolds the RRM tertiary structure.
source: The ANE mutation lies in an α-helix and the mutation disrupts not only the α-helix, but unfolds the RRM tertiary structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by the structural data in Figure 7.

claim: A subset of Nop4 interactions may be mediated by unstructured peptide elements in RRM3 or by the RRM4 domain.
source: Since the mutation abrogates some but not all protein-protein interactions, a subset of Nop4 interactions may be mediated by unstructured peptide elements in RRM3 or by the RRM4 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is speculation based on the observation that not all interactions are disrupted.

claim: Fibroblasts from patients with ANE syndrome have ribosome levels reduced to approximately 60% of controls.
source: Fibroblasts from patients with ANE syndrome have ribosome levels reduced to approximately 60% of controls (Nousbeck et al., 2008), consistent with the modest defects in ribosome biogenesis that we can now associate with the ANE syndrome mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Nousbeck et al., 2008.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation confers reduced growth and mild pre-rRNA processing defects when compared to the Nop4 null in the yeast model system.
source: In the yeast model system, the mutation confers reduced growth and mild pre-rRNA processing defects when compared to the Nop4 null (EV).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The ANE syndrome mutation is a hypomorphic allele.
source: Thus, the ANE syndrome mutation is a hypomorphic allele, consistent with its autosomal recessive inheritance (Nousbeck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is an inference based on the observed phenotypes and inheritance pattern.

claim: The hypomorphism of the ANE syndrome mutation may, in part, explain how the mutation is compatible with life.
source: This hypomorphism may, in part, explain how the ANE syndrome mutation is compatible with life, as the presence of the mutation leads to a partially functional RBM28 protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is speculation based on the hypomorphic nature of the mutation.

claim: The presence of the ANE syndrome mutation leads to a partially functional RBM28 protein.
source: This hypomorphism may, in part, explain how the ANE syndrome mutation is compatible with life, as the presence of the mutation leads to a partially functional RBM28 protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is an inference based on the observed partial complementation in yeast.

claim: Human RBM28 can complement the growth defect in yeast when its ortholog, Nop4, is depleted.
source: Human RBM28 can complement the growth defect in the yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, when its ortholog, the essential Nop4 protein, is depleted (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Kachroo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to Kachroo et al., 2015.

claim: Over their entire length, the amino acid sequences of Nop4 and RBM28 are ~26% identical and 34% similar.
source: Over their entire length, the amino acid sequences of Nop4 and RBM28 are ~26% identical and 34% similar, and both contain four RRMs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Nop4 interacts with 23 large subunit assembly factors with high confidence.
source: Table 1. Nop4 interacts with 23 large subunit assembly factors with high confidence. The Nop4 interacting proteins were identified by yeast two-hybrid and were assigned a confidence score in (McCann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 and supported by citation to McCann et al., 2015.
